signal.title: v1.19.3: WireGuard handshakes never complete on any node pair (tunnel/geneve + DSR), all cross-node pod traffic dead, on Oracle Linux only.
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? After upgrading to Cilium 1.19.3, all cross-node pod-to-pod connectivity is dead cluster-wide. The root symptom is that the WireGuard handshake never completes between *any* pair of nodes, in *either* direction. Every node reports, for every one of its 5 peers: ``` latest handshake: 0001-01-01T00:00:00.000Z transfer: 0 B received, 9836672 B sent ``` ``` 96: cilium_wg0: <POINTOPOINT,NOARP,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1300 ... RX: bytes packets errors dropped missed mcast 0 0 0 0 0 0 TX: bytes packets errors dropped carrier collsns 44358560 299720 0 2162782 0 0 ``` `cilium-dbg status` shows host connectivity is healthy while the encrypted overlay is completely dead: ``` Cluster health: 1/6 reachable (2026-07-28T13:02:11Z) cl-13-kubesi-worker-0: Host connectivity to 10.47.2.203: ICMP to stack: OK, RTT=297.168µs HTTP to agent: OK, RTT=961.602µs Endpoint connectivity to 10.42.2.197: ICMP to stack: Connection timed out HTTP to agent: Get "http://10.42.2.197:4240/hello": context deadline exceeded ``` With `echo module wireguard +p > /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control` on `controlplane-1`: (pattern repeats like this, no 'receiving' alike messages) ``` [427001.163104] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 3 (10.47.2.217:51871) did not complete after 5 seconds, retrying (try 11) [427001.163232] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Sending handshake initiation to peer 3 (10.47.2.217:51871) [427001.175653] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Sending handshake initiation to peer 1 (10.47.2.194:51871) [427004.235068] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 5 (10.47.3.11:51871) did not complete after 5 seconds, retrying (try 2) [427006.284042] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 3 (10.47.2.217:51871) did not complete after 5 seconds, retrying (try 12) [427006.284054] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 2 (10.47.2.203:51871) did not complete after 5 seconds, retrying (try 18) [427023.178883] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 2 (10.47.2.203:51871) did not complete after 20 attempts, giving up ``` I ran claude on this, here's the output: ## What I have already ruled out I did a fairly deep investigation before filing. The following are all **not** the cause: | Hypothesis | Evidence against | |---|---| | **Public key mismatch** | All 6 nodes' live interface keys match their `CiliumNode` `network.cilium.io/wg-pub-key` annotations exactly, and match the corresponding peer entries on other nodes | | **Wrong endpoints / allowed-ips** | Each peer has `endpoint: <nodeIP>:51871` and `allowed ips: <nodeIP>/32`, which is correct for tunnel mode (geneve-encapsulated outer packet) | | **Clock skew (TAI64N replay rejection)** | Node clocks agree within ~1.8s | | **Cilium BPF dropping packets** | `cilium-dbg monitor --type drop -v` shows nothing during reproduction; `cilium-dbg bpf metrics list` shows no drop reasons other than an unrelated `Unsupported L3 protocol` on IPv6 RouterSolicitation | | **Issue #46100 (fragment tracking)** | No `DROP_FRAG_NOT_FOUND` counter present on any node. Handshake initiations are 148 B, far below any MTU | | **Host firewall** | `iptables` OUTPUT rule `ACCEPT all -- 0.0.0.0/0 10.0.0.0/8 state NEW` covers node-to-node traffic (2.7M packets); no DROP rule counter increments during reproduction | | **rp_filter** | `IPReversePathFilter` stays at 0 across bursts (note: `enp1s0/rp_filter=1`, `all=0`, so effective strict — but it is demonstrably not dropping these) | | **Network fabric blocking UDP** | Disproved by measurement — see below | | **Socket not bound / socket drops** | `ss -unlp` shows `UNCONN 0.0.0.0:51871`; `/proc/net/udp` shows `drops=0` for that socket | ### Measurement showing UDP does traverse the fabric Sending synthetic UDP bursts node-to-node (`worker-0` → `worker-1`, both `10.47.2.0/24`): - Receiver NIC counter (`/proc/net/dev`, counted before BPF): `5,603,727 → 5,608,812` = **+5,085 for 5,000 datagrams sent**. Packets reach the wire and the NIC. - Receiver netfilter INPUT hook, diffing `iptables-save -c` around a 3,000-packet burst to port 51871: ``` DELTA=3371 filter [27595:1956942] -A INPUT -m comment --comment "cilium-feeder: CILIUM_INPUT" -j CILIUM_INPUT DELTA=3361 filter [9070529:4141298931] -A INPUT -j KUBE-FIREWALL DELTA=3371 raw -A PREROUTING -j CILIUM_PRE_raw DELTA=3371 mangle -A PREROUTING -j CILIUM_PRE_mangle DELTA=2999 nat -A PREROUTING -j CILIUM_PRE_nat ``` So synthetic UDP to 51871 is routed for local delivery and passes netfilter without being dropped. Node-to-node TCP and ICMP work normally throughout (confirmed by Cilium's own health prober, RTT ~0.3–1 ms). So: the path carries UDP, the keys are right, nothing visibly drops the packets, and yet no peer ever answers a handshake initiation. ### How can we reproduce the issue? Surprisingly: this setup **works** on Ubuntu-based setup, I found this to be broken only on Oracle Linux 1. RKE2 cluster, 6 nodes (3 control-plane, 3 workers), Oracle Linux 9.8 / UEK kernel. 2. Cilium 1.19.3 with the config below: `routing-mode: tunnel` + `tunnel-protocol: geneve`, `encryption.type=wireguard` (nodeEncryption disabled), kube-proxy replacement with `loadBalancer.mode=dsr` and `dsrDispatch=geneve`. 3. Physical NIC MTU 9000 (happens on different clusters with "regular" MTU of 1500 too) , Cilium `MTU: 1380` (yields `cilium_wg0` MTU 1300). 4. Observe `cilium-dbg debuginfo | grep -A5 'peer:'`, all peers show `latest handshake: 0001-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` and `0 B received`. Relevant Helm values: ```yaml MTU: 1380 encryption: enabled: true type: wireguard tunnelProtocol: geneve kubeProxyReplacement: true loadBalancer: algorithm: maglev dsrDispatch: geneve mode: dsr bpf: masquerade: true hostLegacyRouting: false localRedirectPolicies: enabled: true pmtuDiscovery: enabled: true # or false, doesn't matter, both yield same outcome ``` ### Cilium Version `Cilium: Ok 1.19.3 (v1.19.3-f5eb641b)` ### Kernel Version ``` 5.15.0-322.203.3.4.el9uek.x86_64 ``` ### Kubernetes Version ``` 1.35 (v1.35.5+rke2r2) [linux/amd64] ``` ### Regression Yes. This cluster worked before the upgrade to Cilium 1.19 (version: v1.18.3). Connectivity broke at the upgrade. WireGuard has never completed a single handshake in the current agents' lifetime (4d+ uptime, `latest handshake: never`). ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell KubeProxyReplacement: True [enp1s0 10.47.3.11 fe80::21a:4aff:fe16:1c4 10.47.17.1 (Direct Routing)] CNI Chaining: portmap Cilium: Ok 1.19.3 (v1.19.3-f5eb641b) IPAM: IPv4: 14/126 allocated from 10.42.0.128/25 Routing: Network: Tunnel [geneve] Host: BPF Attach Mode: Legacy TC Device Mode: veth Masquerading: BPF [enp1s0] 10.42.0.128/25 [IPv4: Enabled, IPv6: Disabled] Controller Status: 86/86 healthy Encryption: Wireguard [NodeEncryption: Disabled, cilium_wg0 (Pubkey: 7we7...fjk8=, Port: 51871, Peers: 5)] Cluster health: 1/6 reachable Modules Health: Stopped(23) Degraded(0) OK(113) ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: Cilium datapath drops on OCP 4.22 breaks DNS/apiserver connectivity
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.20.0 and lower than v1.21.0 ### What happened? We install Cilium 1.20.0 via Helm as the CNI on a HyperShift-based OpenShift (OCP) hosted cluster. On **OCP 4.22** worker nodes, after Cilium comes up, in-cluster DNS resolution never stabilizes: • CoreDNS pods stay 1/2 Ready, continuously logging: ``` [ERROR] plugin/kubernetes: Failed to watch [WARNING] plugin/kubernetes: starting server with unsynced Kubernetes API ``` • Cluster operators dns , console , and ingress never reach Available=True (dns reports "DNS default is unavailable"; console reports `dial udp 172.30.0.10:53: connect: operation not permitted`). • Cilium's own `cilium-connectivity-check-*` test pods CrashLoopBackOff with `curl: (28) Resolving timed out`. The same Helm chart/values on OCP 4.20 worker nodes works correctly — DNS and all cluster operators become available normally. The only variable changed between the working and broken runs is the OCP/RHCOS version of the worker node (4.20 → 4.22); no other test/config change was made. Inspecting the `kube-apiserver-proxy` (haproxy) access log on the host confirmed the problem is at the **datapath level, not the service-programming level**: • CoreDNS's pod IP never appears at all in the haproxy access log — its connection attempts toward `172.20.0.1:6443` never reach the host side, i.e. they are dropped somewhere between the pod veth and the host network namespace. • Other pods' connections that do eventually get through show a recurring ~90 second stall before completing (haproxy timer tuple like `1/1/90022` ), i.e. severe latency/retries rather than a clean failure. This points to a Cilium eBPF/datapath incompatibility with the newer RHCOS kernel shipped in OCP 4.22, rather than a Helm-chart configuration issue on our side, since toggling kube-proxy-replacement made no difference. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Provision an OpenShift 4.22 cluster (we use HyperShift-based ARO-HCP, but the underlying issue should reproduce on any 4.22 cluster where the host-networked apiserver endpoint is not the primary Service ClusterIP path, or more generally wherever this pod→host datapath is exercised). 2. Disable OpenShift's built-in kube-proxy: `oc patch network.operator.openshift.io cluster --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"deployKubeProxy":false}}'` 3. Install Cilium 1.20.0 via Helm with (abbreviated) values: ``` debug: enabled: true k8s: requireIPv4PodCIDR: true logSystemLoad: true bpf: preallocateMaps: true ipv4: enabled: true ipv6: enabled: false identityChangeGracePeriod: "0s" ipam: mode: cluster-pool operator: clusterPoolIPv4PodCIDRList: ["<pod CIDR>"] clusterPoolIPv4MaskSize: <host prefix> endpointRoutes: enabled: true tunnelPort: 4789 cni: binPath: /var/lib/cni/bin confPath: /var/run/multus/cni/net.d chainingMode: portmap kubeProxyReplacement: true k8sServiceHost: "172.20.0.1" # host-networked apiserver proxy IP in our env k8sServicePort: 6443 ``` 4. Add a worker node pool; wait for nodes to become `Ready` and Cilium DaemonSet pods `Running` . 5. Observe: CoreDNS pods never reach `2/2` Ready; `oc get co dns` stays `Available=False` ; `cilium-connectivity-check-*` test pods crash-loop. 6. Cross-check: repeat steps 1–5 against an OCP 4.20 worker node with identical Helm values — this succeeds cleanly, all operators become `Available=True` . **Additional diagnostics gathered:** • `cilium-agent` debug logs confirm correct service/backend/RevNat programming for `default/kubernetes` (ClusterIP `172.30.0.1:443` → backend `172.20.0.1:6443` ). • Host-side haproxy access logs for the apiserver-proxy show CoreDNS's pod IP never arriving, and other pods' connections stalling ~90s before completing. Happy to provide full `cilium-agent` debug logs, `cilium-dbg service list` / BPF map dumps, and exact kernel version from a fresh repro if that would help — let me know what additional info/access would be most useful. ### Cilium Version 1.20.0 ### Kernel Version 5.14.0-687.39.1.el9_8.x86_64 (RHCOS 9.8) ### Kubernetes Version v1.35.6 (OCP 4.22.10 control plane; kubelet/kube-proxy also v1.35.6 on the node) ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: api: Type the MAC fields as `mac.MAC`
signal.text: The five MAC fields in the agent API were plain strings that every consumer immediately parsed. This PR types them with `x-go-type`, the same way 99d9d398fc did for `Address` and `CIDR`, so the model carries the semantic type and the round-trip noise disappears. There are also two setup commits to help with that: one making `pkg/mac` a leaf package, so that `api/v1/models` can import it without dragging in netlink and k8s dependencies, and another commit typing `ipam.AllocationResult.PrimaryMAC` so the master interface MAC is parsed once on entry rather than on every use. See the individual commits message for details.
signal.author: HadrienPatte

signal.title: cilium-agent <-> cilium-envoy livelock on cilium.NetworkPolicy xDS after upgrading to 1.20.0 — sustained 85-100% CPU on every node, no CiliumNetworkPolicy/CiliumEnvoyConfig present
signal.text: ## Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues. Closest match I found is #43770 ("CI: Conformance L7-only (ci-l7): connection disruption during agent restart") — same `agent.controlplane.envoy-proxy` / `cilium.NetworkPolicy` xDS code path and affects v1.19/v1.20, but that one is a restart-time race that self-resolves within ~3-4 minutes via the policy-restore fallback timeout. What we hit did not involve an agent restart and did not self-resolve (ran at 85-100% CPU for 40+ minutes until we manually restarted the pods). Flagging both here in case they share a root cause, but filing separately since the trigger and recovery behavior differ. ## Version equal or higher than v1.20.0 and lower than v1.21.0 ## What happened? About 13 hours after a clean upgrade from 1.19.6 to 1.20.0 (Helm chart_version bumped in lockstep with the image tag, DaemonSet rolled 6/6 nodes with no errors, `cilium connectivity test` passed clean before and after with no new failures), all 3 worker nodes in a 6-node cluster (3 control-plane, 3 workers) climbed to 85-100% CPU, sustained, with no change in actual traffic pattern. Root cause turned out to be cilium-agent and its embedded cilium-envoy stuck in an unbounded xDS request/response loop over the `type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy` resource: - cilium-agent logs showed continuous `OnStreamRequest`/`OnStreamResponse` pairs (module=`agent.controlplane.envoy-proxy`), with `xdsNonce` incrementing forever and never converging — e.g. nonce went from 6421447 to 6421520 (73 increments) within about 180ms in one sample window. A 10-second log capture on one node's agent contained 44,950 `OnStream*` log lines (~4,495/sec). - The corresponding cilium-envoy container logged `Ignoring unwatched type URL type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy` (grpc_mux_impl.cc:396) continuously, every 3-5ms, forever. - Two xDS version hashes were involved throughout and never matched: the agent kept serving `xdsVersion=f494f7846` while envoy kept requesting against `xdsVersion=5dc77ff454`. - This happened with **zero** `CiliumNetworkPolicy`, `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy`, `NetworkPolicy`, or `CiliumEnvoyConfig` objects present anywhere in the cluster. The only thing enabling L7/Envoy involvement is `hubble.metrics` including `httpV2` (L7 HTTP visibility) — that config predates this upgrade and was untouched by it. - Control-plane nodes (which don't run this cilium-agent DaemonSet workload the same way / weren't under similar churn) were unaffected the entire time — CPU stayed at 8-15%. The timing correlated with — but as far as we can tell wasn't directly caused by — an unrelated pod churn event on the cluster (a healthcheck controller's periodic DaemonSet/Deployment/DNS check pods being created and torn down on a ~20-30 minute cycle). Our working theory is that this churn triggered enough endpoint/policy recomputation to tip an already-fragile 1.20.0 xDS reconciliation into the livelock, but we don't have a minimal repro yet. **Expected behavior**: cilium-agent and cilium-envoy's xDS NetworkPolicy stream should converge to a stable version and go quiet absent further policy/endpoint changes, as it did under 1.19.6. ## How can we reproduce the issue? We don't have a minimal repro yet — this took ~13 hours of real cluster uptime plus what we believe was a churn trigger to manifest, and it did not reproduce immediately after the initial upgrade/rollout verification. Our environment, for context: 1. 6-node bare-metal/VM cluster (3 control-plane, 3 workers), Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8.0-136-generic. 2. Cilium installed via Helm (`chart_ref: cilium/cilium`, `chart_version` == app version, always in lockstep). 3. Relevant Helm values: `ipv6.enabled: true` / `ipv4.enabled: false` (IPv6-only), `routingMode: native`, `kubeProxyReplacement: true`, `hubble.enabled: true` with `hubble.metrics.enabled` including `httpV2`, `bgpControlPlane.enabled: true`. 4. No `CiliumNetworkPolicy`/`CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy`/`NetworkPolicy`/`CiliumEnvoyConfig` objects defined anywhere in the cluster. 5. Upgraded `cilium_version` 1.19.6 -> 1.20.0 via `helm upgrade`. Rollout itself was clean (verified via `cilium status`, `hubble status`, and `cilium connectivity test` pre/post). 6. ~13 hours later, worker-node CPU began climbing, fully saturating over roughly 10-15 minutes, coincident with unrelated pod churn elsewhere in the cluster. **Workaround**: a full restart of cilium-agent + cilium-envoy (we used a node reboot, since `kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets` intentionally leaves DaemonSet pods running and a plain pod delete would likely work too but we didn't test that specifically) immediately cleared the loop — CPU dropped from 85-100% to 9-11% within about a minute, and the xDS request rate returned to a handful of requests per 15 seconds (normal baseline) on all three affected nodes. This is a workaround, not a fix — the underlying condition is presumably still reachable and could recur on the next churn event. ## Cilium Version ``` Client: 1.20.0 450c5314 2026-07-29T08:53:01+02:00 go version go1.26.5 linux/amd64 Daemon: 1.20.0 450c5314 2026-07-29T08:53:01+02:00 go version go1.26.5 linux/amd64 ``` Image: `quay.io/cilium/cilium:v1.20.0@sha256:383968cd5e8873f7976fa76aa6196045643558f4cc9518a207b9335cb24a0e93` ## Kernel Version ``` Linux node-0 6.8.0-136-generic #136-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Wed Jul 1 21:53:05 UTC 2026 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux ``` ## Kubernetes Version ``` Client Version: v1.36.3 Server Version: v1.36.3 ``` ## Regression Yes. Cluster ran on 1.19.6 for an extended period without this issue. Only started after upgrading to 1.20.0, and only manifested ~13 hours post-upgrade rather than immediately. ## Sysdump Not captured at the time — we didn't realize the significance until CPU was already saturated and prioritized restoring service. Happy to attempt to reproduce and capture one in a maintenance window if that would help, since the fix-by-reboot workaround means we can safely force the condition again if there's a reliable way to trigger the churn that seems to precede it. ## Relevant log output cilium-agent (module=agent.controlplane.envoy-proxy), representative sample — this pattern repeated continuously for 40+ minutes until the pod was restarted: ``` time=2026-07-30T19:25:09.729497532Z level=info msg=OnStreamResponse module=agent.controlplane.envoy-proxy xdsStreamID=1 xdsVersion=f494f7846 xdsTypeURL=type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy numResources=4 time=2026-07-30T19:25:09.731345892Z level=info msg=OnStreamRequest module=agent.controlplane.envoy-proxy xdsStreamID=1 xdsVersion=5dc77ff454 xdsTypeURL=type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy xdsNonce=6421447 xdsResourceNames=[] time=2026-07-30T19:25:09.731445216Z level=info msg=OnStreamResponse module=agent.controlplane.envoy-proxy xdsStreamID=1 xdsVersion=f494f7846 xdsTypeURL=type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy numResources=4 time=2026-07-30T19:25:09.732050553Z level=info msg=OnStreamRequest module=agent.controlplane.envoy-proxy xdsStreamID=1 xdsVersion=5dc77ff454 xdsTypeURL=type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy xdsNonce=6421448 xdsResourceNames=[] time=2026-07-30T19:25:09.910705584Z level=info msg=OnStreamRequest module=agent.controlplane.envoy-proxy xdsStreamID=1 xdsVersion=5dc77ff454 xdsTypeURL=type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy xdsNonce=6421520 xdsResourceNames=[] ``` cilium-envoy, same time window: ``` [2026-07-30 19:26:16.806][7][warning][config] [external/envoy/source/extensions/config_subscription/grpc/grpc_mux_impl.cc:396] Ignoring unwatched type URL type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy [2026-07-30 19:26:16.813][7][warning][config] [external/envoy/source/extensions/config_subscription/grpc/grpc_mux_impl.cc:396] Ignoring unwatched type URL type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy [2026-07-30 19:26:16.819][7][warning][config] [external/envoy/source/extensions/config_subscription/grpc/grpc_mux_impl.cc:396] Ignoring unwatched type URL type.googleapis.com/cilium.NetworkPolicy ``` (repeating every 3-5ms, indefinitely) `kubectl top nodes` before / after the workaround reboot (worker nodes only): ``` node-0 997m (99%) -> 106m (10%) node-1 999m (99%) -> 112m (11%) node-2 1702m (85%) -> 82m (4%) ``` ## Anything else? Possibly related: #43770 discusses a chicken-and-egg fence between `CiliumEnvoyConfig` initialization and the Envoy xDS server waiting on initial policy computation during endpoint regeneration, in the same `agent.controlplane.envoy-proxy` / `cilium.NetworkPolicy` code path. We don't use `CiliumEnvoyConfig` at all, so if these share a root cause it's likely in the more general Envoy NetworkPolicy xDS reconciliation logic rather than the CiliumEnvoyConfig-specific fence path described there. - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? signal.title: L7 CiliumNetworkPolicy: ingress proxy upstream leg never completes — pod's SYN-ACK reaches the veth but not the host stack (1.20.0, kernel 6.1, tunnel/vxlan)
signal.text: ## Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ## What happened? When any L7 `CiliumNetworkPolicy` is attached to an endpoint, the **ingress proxy's upstream leg (Envoy → backend pod) never completes its TCP handshake**, and the affected Service becomes unreachable for as long as the policy exists. Removing the policy restores it instantly. The downstream leg works correctly: eBPF marks the packet, `iptables` TPROXY redirects it, Envoy's transparent socket accepts it, Envoy parses the HTTP request, and Hubble emits an `http-request FORWARDED` flow. Only the leg **after** that fails. ``` client ──► eBPF mark ──► iptables TPROXY ──► Envoy transparent socket ──► HTTP parse ──► Hubble L7 flow OK OK OK 36 pkts OK cx_total 9 OK OK │ Envoy ──► backend pod ◄──────────────────────┘ FAIL: SYN sent, pod replies SYN-ACK on the lxc veth, but the SYN-ACK never reaches the host stack. RST after ~2s. 26/26 = 100%. ``` `envoy_cluster_upstream_cx_connect_timeout{envoy_cluster_name="ingress-cluster"}` equals `envoy_cluster_upstream_cx_total` — **every** upstream connection times out. Critically, `cilium-dbg monitor --type drop` reports **zero drops**, so the packet is lost silently somewhere between the veth ingress and the host network stack. This looks closely related to how the ingress proxy's upstream connection is classified in conntrack — see **Possible root cause** below. ### tcpdump — the failing leg, with a working control in the same capture Captured with `tcpdump -i any -e -n` in the host netns. The full pcap is attached. **Control — before the policy is applied.** Same source IP, same pod, same veth: ``` 12:55:09.853371 lxcc4bd6dbfdc72 Out 10.42.0.213.55556 > 10.42.0.204.9187: Flags [S] 12:55:09.853388 lxcc4bd6dbfdc72 In 10.42.0.204.9187 > 10.42.0.213.55556: Flags [S.] 12:55:09.853414 lxcc4bd6dbfdc72 Out 10.42.0.213.55556 > 10.42.0.204.9187: Flags [.], ack 1 ^ the ACK goes out, i.e. the host stack received the SYN-ACK. Connection proceeds normally. ``` **Downstream leg with the policy applied — works.** This is the kubelet HTTP readiness probe being TPROXY-redirected into Envoy: ``` 12:55:24.853830 cilium_host Out 10.42.0.213.49598 > 10.42.0.204.9187: Flags [S] 12:55:24.853849 lo In 10.42.0.204.9187 > 10.42.0.213.49598: Flags [S.] ^ Envoy's transparent socket answers on lo, spoofing the pod address 12:55:24.853936 cilium_host Out 10.42.0.213.49598 > 10.42.0.204.9187: Flags [P.], length 110 ^ GET /metrics HTTP/1.1 12:55:25.854421 cilium_host Out ... Flags [F.] (kubelet timeoutSeconds: 1 gives up) ``` **Upstream leg with the policy applied — fails.** This is Envoy connecting to the backend pod: ``` 12:55:24.854560 lxcc4bd6dbfdc72 Out 10.42.0.213.49608 > 10.42.0.204.9187: Flags [S] 12:55:24.854572 lxcc4bd6dbfdc72 In 10.42.0.204.9187 > 10.42.0.213.49608: Flags [S.] ^ the pod answers correctly, the SYN-ACK reaches the veth ... ^ ... and is never seen again. It appears on NEITHER cilium_host NOR lo. 12:55:25.879008 lxcc4bd6dbfdc72 Out 10.42.0.213.49608 > ...: Flags [S] (retransmit) 12:55:25.879027 lxcc4bd6dbfdc72 In 10.42.0.204.9187 > ...: Flags [S.] 12:55:27.891029 lxcc4bd6dbfdc72 In 10.42.0.204.9187 > ...: Flags [S.] 12:55:27.891099 cilium_host Out 10.42.0.213.49608 > ...: Flags [R] (RST, ~3s in) ``` The contrast between the control and the failing leg is the core of this report: **the identical path (same veth, same source IP, same destination pod) works without the policy and drops the SYN-ACK with it.** ### conntrack — only `ProxyRedirect` entries never see return traffic ``` $ cilium-dbg bpf ct list global | grep '10.42.0.204:9187' # with the L7 policy attached: TCP IN 10.42.0.213:49598 -> 10.42.0.204:9187 RxFlagsSeen=0x1b TxFlagsSeen=0x00 \ Flags=0x0051 [ RxClosing SeenNonSyn ProxyRedirect ] TCP IN 10.42.0.213:53672 -> 10.42.0.204:9187 RxFlagsSeen=0x1b TxFlagsSeen=0x00 \ Flags=0x0051 [ RxClosing SeenNonSyn ProxyRedirect ] TCP IN 10.42.0.213:39982 -> 10.42.0.204:9187 RxFlagsSeen=0x1b TxFlagsSeen=0x00 \ Flags=0x0051 [ RxClosing SeenNonSyn ProxyRedirect ] # same pod, before the policy was attached: TCP IN 10.42.0.213:47702 -> 10.42.0.204:9187 RxFlagsSeen=0x1f TxFlagsSeen=0x1a \ Flags=0x0013 [ RxClosing TxClosing SeenNonSyn ] TCP IN 10.42.0.213:60840 -> 10.42.0.204:9187 RxFlagsSeen=0x1f TxFlagsSeen=0x1a \ Flags=0x0013 [ RxClosing TxClosing SeenNonSyn ] ``` Every entry carrying `ProxyRedirect` has `TxFlagsSeen=0x00` — no return traffic ever observed. Every entry without it has `TxFlagsSeen=0x1a`. No exceptions. ### Envoy metrics (read from the Prometheus endpoint on `:9964`) ``` envoy_listener_downstream_cx_total{envoy_listener_address="127.0.0.1_10488"} 9 envoy_http_downstream_cx_total{envoy_http_conn_manager_prefix="proxy"} 9 envoy_http_downstream_rq_total{envoy_http_conn_manager_prefix="proxy"} 9 envoy_http_downstream_rq_rx_reset{envoy_http_conn_manager_prefix="proxy"} 9 envoy_cluster_upstream_cx_total{envoy_cluster_name="ingress-cluster"} 26 envoy_cluster_upstream_cx_connect_fail{envoy_cluster_name="ingress-cluster"} 26 envoy_cluster_upstream_cx_connect_timeout{envoy_cluster_name="ingress-cluster"} 26 ``` Envoy accepts and parses fine; 100% of upstream connections time out. The `rx_reset` count reflects the kubelet probe (`timeoutSeconds: 1`) resetting before Envoy's upstream timeout elapses — with a client that waits longer, Envoy returns `503 upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers ... connection timeout`. ### Hubble confirms the request reaches L7 ``` $ hubble observe --protocol http Aug 5 12:56:10.856: 10.42.0.213:41478 (host) -> forge/postgres-exporter-...:9187 (ID:54041) \ http-request FORWARDED (HTTP/1.1 GET http://10.42.0.204:9187/metrics) ``` Because no response is ever produced, `hubble_http_requests_total` stays at zero series — the httpV2 handler only emits on responses. This makes the failure additionally hard to spot from metrics alone. ### Ruled out by measurement | Hypothesis | How it was checked | Result | |---|---|---| | Envoy's listening socket is not `IP_TRANSPARENT` | `ss -lnptOe --inet-sockopt` in the host netns | **transparent is set** on all 4 worker sockets (`fwmark:0xa00`) | | Proxy port mismatch / stale redirect | `cilium-dbg status --all-redirects`, `iptables-save -t mangle`, Envoy listener dump | all `10488`, exactly one redirect | | Missing kernel modules | `/proc/modules` | `xt_TPROXY`, `xt_socket`, `nf_tproxy_ipv4/v6`, `nf_socket_ipv4/v6`, `nf_defrag_ipv4/v6` all loaded | | Envoy / iptables in different netns | `readlink /proc/self/ns/net` | identical (`net:[4026531840]`) | | Host firewall (ufw) eating proxy traffic | `CILIUM_INPUT` vs `INPUT` policy DROP deltas in a window where TPROXY fired 36 pkts | `CILIUM_INPUT` ACCEPT +43, `INPUT` DROP +3 (background rate). Not ufw. | | Policy enforcement / default-deny | `enableDefaultDeny: {ingress: false, egress: false}` visibility-only policy | **identical failure** | | eBPF explicitly dropping | `cilium-dbg monitor --type drop` | 0 drops | | Kernel rejecting the connection | `nstat`: `ListenDrops`, `ListenOverflows`, `TCPReqQFullDrop`, `TcpAttemptFails` | all unchanged during failure | | xDS delivery | agent + Envoy logs | `lds: add/update listener 'cilium-http-ingress:10488'` on every attach | | Standalone vs embedded Envoy | tested both | fails in both (embedded surfaces it as a 503 because clients wait long enough) | | `rp_filter` | `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/*/rp_filter` | all 0 | | Leftover CNI from a previous mesh (Linkerd) | `/etc/cni/net.d`, iptables nat, CRDs | clean | ## Cilium Version ``` Client: 1.20.0 450c5314 2026-07-29T08:53:01+02:00 go version go1.26.5 linux/amd64 Daemon: 1.20.0 450c5314 2026-07-29T08:53:01+02:00 go version go1.26.5 linux/amd64 ``` cilium-envoy: `quay.io/cilium/cilium-envoy:v1.37.5-1782911245-7cffc778c923f68a77954a53b1a98d6b5353f004` (`sha256:583057dd4f7d54cd41efff3c413aa0b148ac201f522e2c3336851fa89c78b039`) Note: Kubernetes 1.36 is only supported by Cilium 1.20, so downgrading to test an earlier minor is not an option here. ## Kernel Version ``` Linux 6.1.0-50-amd64 x86_64 GNU/Linux (Debian 12) ``` ## Kubernetes Version ``` Client Version: v1.36.2+k3s1 Server Version: v1.36.2+k3s1 ``` Single node, 4 vCPU / 31 GiB. ## Relevant configuration ``` kube-proxy-replacement true routing-mode tunnel tunnel-protocol vxlan datapath-mode veth ipam cluster-pool identity-allocation-mode crd enable-l7-proxy true external-envoy-proxy true # standalone cilium-envoy DaemonSet (also reproduced with embedded) envoy-xds-mode ads bpf-lb-sock false enable-ipv4-masquerade true enable-bpf-masquerade (unset) # also reproduced with this set to true enable-host-legacy-routing (unset) enable-endpoint-routes (unset) devices (auto) # also reproduced pinned to a single device enable-ipv6 false ``` `cilium-dbg status`: ``` KubeProxyReplacement: True [enp3s0 192.168.219.100 (Direct Routing), tailscale0 100.118.42.102] Routing: Network: Tunnel [vxlan] Host: Legacy Masquerading: IPTables [IPv4: Enabled, IPv6: Disabled] Proxy Status: OK, ip 10.42.0.213, 1 redirects active on ports 10000-20000, Envoy: external Controller Status: 283/283 healthy ``` ## How can we reproduce the issue? **Pick a target that actually receives HTTP traffic.** This matters — I initially used a Service whose readinessProbe was `tcpSocket`, saw `downstream_cx_total = 0`, and wrongly concluded that Envoy was never receiving connections. It was simply never being sent any HTTP. Here I use a `postgres-exporter` whose readinessProbe is `httpGet /metrics` and which is scraped by Prometheus, so requests flow continuously. **1. Baseline** ```bash kubectl -n forge run probe --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.5.0 -- \ -sS --max-time 8 -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code} connect %{time_connect}s\n" \ http://postgres-exporter:9187/metrics # HTTP 200 connect 0.000613s ``` **2. Attach a visibility-only L7 policy** (no enforcement — `enableDefaultDeny` disabled in both directions, so this changes nothing except turning on L7 parsing) ```yaml apiVersion: cilium.io/v2 kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy metadata: name: l7-vis-postgres-exporter namespace: forge spec: endpointSelector: matchLabels: app: postgres-exporter enableDefaultDeny: ingress: false egress: false ingress: - fromEntities: - all toPorts: - ports: - port: "9187" protocol: TCP rules: http: - {} ``` **3. Observe** ```bash # the redirect and listener come up cleanly kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -c cilium-agent -- cilium-dbg status --all-redirects | grep -A2 'Proxy Port' # cilium-http-ingress 856:ingress:TCP:9187: 10488 kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/cilium-envoy | grep lds # lds: add/update listener 'cilium-http-ingress:10488' # Envoy accepts and parses, but every upstream connection times out curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9964/metrics | grep -E 'ingress-cluster.*(connect_fail|connect_timeout|cx_total)' # conntrack: ProxyRedirect entries never see return traffic kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -c cilium-agent -- cilium-dbg bpf ct list global | grep ProxyRedirect # no eBPF drops are reported kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -c cilium-agent -- cilium-dbg monitor --type drop ``` The Service is unreachable for as long as the policy exists; the pod goes `0/1` because its HTTP readiness probe now fails. **4. Remove the policy — recovery is immediate** (`HTTP 200`, ~0.6 ms). Reproduced 100% of the time across many attempts, on `admin-front:3000` and `postgres-exporter:9187`, with standalone and embedded Envoy, with and without `bpf.masquerade`, with `devices` auto-detected and pinned. ### Capturing the packet trace The node's `ss` was too old for `--inet-sockopt` (iproute2 6.1.0; the option needs 6.4+), so I ran the socket and packet inspection from a netshoot pod sharing the host netns: ```bash kubectl -n kube-system run netshoot-diag --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never \ --overrides='{"spec":{"hostNetwork":true,"hostPID":true, "containers":[{"name":"netshoot","image":"nicolaka/netshoot","command":["sleep","3600"], "securityContext":{"privileged":true}}]}}' kubectl -n kube-system exec netshoot-diag -- \ tcpdump -i any -e -n "tcp port 9187 or tcp portrange 10000-20000" -w /tmp/l7.pcap ``` One note for anyone else chasing this: `tcpdump port 10488` will **always** be empty. TPROXY hands the packet to the socket without rewriting the destination, so no packet ever carries `127.0.0.1:10488` as an address. I lost time on this assumption. ## Possible root cause I have not confirmed this in the datapath code, and I would appreciate a maintainer pointing me at the right place — I am happy to write the fix once the code path is identified. **The ingress proxy's upstream connection is 5-tuple-shaped like the downstream connection it is serving, and the return traffic appears to be classified as proxy-redirect traffic a second time.** Because `cilium-envoy` runs in the host netns, its upstream connection to the backend uses the `cilium_host` address as source. In this cluster that is `10.42.0.213`, which is also the source address of the host-originated traffic being proxied. So both legs look like: ``` downstream (client → proxy): 10.42.0.213:49598 → 10.42.0.204:9187 upstream (proxy → backend): 10.42.0.213:49608 → 10.42.0.204:9187 ``` They differ only in source port. Both create `TCP IN` conntrack entries toward the same `dst:dport`, and in the captured state **both** carry the `ProxyRedirect` flag while neither records any return traffic (`TxFlagsSeen=0x00`). My working hypothesis is that when the pod's SYN-ACK enters `from-container` on the lxc veth, the reverse-direction CT lookup matches an entry marked `ProxyRedirect` and the packet is steered toward the proxy instead of being delivered to the host stack where Envoy's client socket is waiting. That would explain every observation at once: - the SYN-ACK is visible on the veth but on neither `cilium_host` nor `lo` - no drop is reported (the packet is redirected, not dropped) - kernel TCP rejection counters stay flat (it is non-delivery, not refusal) - the downstream leg is unaffected (it is the direction the redirect is meant for) - removing the policy — and with it the `ProxyRedirect` classification — fixes it instantly If that is right, the fix would live in how Envoy's upstream socket mark (`MARK_MAGIC_PROXY_INGRESS`, `0xa00`, which `ss` confirms is set on the listening socket) is expected to exempt the connection from re-redirection, and why that exemption is not taking effect on the return path here. It is possible this only manifests in the specific combination below, which is why I have listed it explicitly: - `routing-mode: tunnel` (vxlan) **combined with** `KubeProxyReplacement` reporting `Direct Routing` - `enable-bpf-masquerade` unset, so `Routing: Host: Legacy` and `Masquerading: IPTables` — an unusual pairing with `kube-proxy-replacement: true`. I also reproduced it with `bpf.masquerade: true` (`Host: BPF`), so this does not appear to be the trigger, but the two paths differ enough to be worth checking. - `bpf-lb-sock: false` Happy to run any additional instrumentation on this cluster — it is a lab node and I can attach the policy and break it at will. ## Anything else? **Attachments** (I will attach these to the issue directly): - `cilium-sysdump-during-failure.zip` — sysdump taken **while the policy was attached and failing**, so it contains the failing CT entries and Envoy stats - `l7-upstream-leg-failure.pcap` — the full `tcpdump -i any -e` capture containing both the working control and the failing upstream leg **Impact.** L7 features are unusable on this cluster: no L7 policy, and no `hubble_http_*` metrics, since requests never produce responses. Attaching a policy to get metrics takes the Service down, and the only status code it would ever record is `503`. L3/L4 policy, flow visibility, `hubble_flows_processed_total`, `hubble_tcp_flags_total` and the service map all work normally.

signal.title: Envoy NPDS not updated when new identities are added for GatewayAPI ingress endpoints doing hairpin traffic for (at least) wildcard matching policies
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.18.5 and lower than v1.19.0 ### What happened? When using Gateway API with L7LB services, hairpin traffic from cluster-internal workloads (e.g., uptime-kuma self-monitoring) to gateway endpoints is intermittently denied by Envoy with "403 Access denied". The issue will crop up sometimes after a cluster-internal workload being monitored is rescheduled. The new backend identity is correctly added to the Cilium agent's policy for the ingress endpoint (visible in `cilium-dbg endpoint get <ingress-endpoint-id>`), but the local Envoy's NPDS is not updated. Envoy denies traffic with: ``` cilium.network: No policy found for id: <identity> ``` **Expected behavior:** When a new identity is added to the selector cache, the ingress endpoint's Envoy NPDS should be updated to include the new identity, allowing traffic to flow. **Actual behavior:** The NPDS remains stale until either: 1. A config change triggers a full policy regeneration on the affected node 2. The cilium-agent pod is restarted 3. A policy change triggers an update of the `reserved:ingress` endpoint and up-to-date identities are pushed. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Deploy Gateway API with HTTPRoutes pointing to backend services on Node A. I'm using Cilium LBIPAM to back the Gateway in this case. 2. Apply a ClusterwideCiliumPolicy that allows traffic from the ingress entity for all relevant workloads that uses an `endpointSelector: {}` selector (so that it ADDITIONALLY matches reserved:ingress). For example a wide-open policy like: ``` spec: egress: - toEntities: - world - remote-node - cluster - kube-apiserver - toEndpoints: - {} endpointSelector: {} ingress: - fromEntities: - world - cluster - remote-node - kube-apiserver - ingress - fromEndpoints: - {} ``` 3. Deploy a monitoring workload (e.g., uptime-kuma) on Node B that performs hairpin requests to services through the gateway's external IP 5. Scale down and up (or delete/recreate) a backend pod that the gateway routes to (e.g. migrate it from Node A to Node C) 6. The new backend pod gets a new identity 7. Hairpin traffic from the monitoring workload to the gateway is denied with 403. In this case I'll see something like the following running when running `cilium-dbg endpoint get [reserved:ingress's identity] |grep revision` on Node A: before restarting the backend: ``` "proxy-policy-revision": 25 "policy-revision": 25 ``` after restarting the backend: ``` "proxy-policy-revision": 25 "policy-revision": 26 ``` and the cilium-agent will have the new identities for the backend workload, but envoy will not have received them. However the issue does not always seem to trigger, probably because of other simultaneous changes that force envoy to be updated with the new identities. But it's often enough to be problematic beyond monitoring (e.g. cert-manager HTTP-01 lets-encrypt challenges' self-check before submission). ### Cilium Version ``` Client: 1.18.5 7d4d8932 2025-12-17T04:56:47+00:00 go version go1.24.11 linux/amd64 Daemon: 1.18.5 7d4d8932 2025-12-17T04:56:47+00:00 go version go1.24.11 linux/amd64 ``` But I have been having this issue intermittently since I began using Gateway API circa Cilium 1.16 ### Kernel Version ``` Linux 6.18.1-talos #1 SMP Wed Dec 17 10:07:33 UTC 2025 x86_64 Linux (Talos 1.12.0) ``` ### Kubernetes Version ``` Client Version: v1.35.0 Server Version: v1.35.0 ``` ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### Anything else? ### Root Cause Analysis Based on code analysis (thanks claude-code plus finally having enough free time to really dig in), the issue appears to be in `/pkg/endpoint/bpf.go` in `applyPolicyMapChangesLocked`: ```go // Line 1093-1094 updateEnvoy := hasNewPolicy // FALSE for incremental identity updates // Line 1115-1128 if !changes.Empty() { // updateEnvoy if there were any mapChanges, but only if the endpoint has Envoy // redirects, or is an Ingress endpoint updateEnvoy = updateEnvoy || hasEnvoyRedirect || e.isIngress } ``` The issue appears to be that `updateEnvoy` is only set to `true` if `!changes.Empty()` is TRUE **first**. For wildcard selectors, it seems no map changes are accumulated because of an early return in `/pkg/policy/l4.go`: ```go // Line 815-816 if cs.IsWildcard() { return // No AccumulateMapChanges called! } ``` The ingress endpoint appears to use wildcard selectors (via `wildcardRule` in `repository.go:463-470`). If this analysis is correct, when new identities are added: 1. `SelectorCache.UpdateIdentities` is called 2. The wildcard selector is notified via `IdentitySelectionUpdated` 3. Early return at line 815-816 because `cs.IsWildcard()` is true 4. No map changes are accumulated 5. In `applyPolicyMapChangesLocked`, `changes.Empty()` returns TRUE 6. `updateEnvoy` is never set despite `e.isIngress` being TRUE 7. `UpdateNetworkPolicy` is never called 8. Envoy NPDS remains stale There may be other factors contributing to this issue that contribute to the issue but haven't yet identified. ### Why this matters for L7LB/Gateway traffic L7LB services like GatewayAPI cause the hairpin traffic to be diverted to the source's **local** Envoy on the source node, which now potentially has stale identities. This means: - Traffic from a monitoring pod on node-A to the gateway IP is redirected to node-A's local Envoy - Node-A's Envoy checks the local ingress endpoint's (reserved:ingress) policy - If the backend's identity is missing from node-A's ingress endpoint NPDS, traffic is denied The ingress endpoint exists on every node with potentially different states if NPDS updates are not triggered. ### Possible Fix Direction If the analysis above is correct, one potential fix might be to modify the condition at line 1115-1128 to trigger Envoy updates for ingress endpoints when there's a new selector snapshot, regardless of whether map changes are empty. However, I don't pretend to understand the cilium architecture well enough; perhaps some other mechanism should also be updating envoy identity data and isn't being triggered in the case of hairpin traffic. ### Workaround Triggering any config change on the affected node's cilium-agent (e.g., toggling debug logging) causes a full policy regeneration which includes calling `UpdateNetworkPolicy` for the ingress endpoint, updating the NPDS with the new identities. ### Cilium Users Document - [x] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: operator: Emit startup logs in the configured log format
signal.text: The operator derives its subsystem logger from `logging.DefaultSlogLogger` before `initEnv()` ran, i.e. before `SetupLogging()` applies the user's `--log-opt` format. `slog.Logger.With()` snapshots the handler it derives from, and `multiSlogHandler.WithAttrs()` copies the current handler list, so the later `SetHandler()` call does not reach the derived logger: the registered-options dump and the version line get emitted in the default text format while everything else respects the user supplied logging config. The derived logger also misses the metrics logging hook registered by `AddHandlers()`. With this change, we derive the logger once the logging setup is complete, like the agent already does. How the operator behaves today when started with `--log-opt='format=json-ts'"`: We can see that the flags dump as well as the "Cilium Operator" logs are emitted as plain text (default logger) before the logger gets properly configured and following logs get properly JSON formatted. And with this patch: Note: I checked the other binaries in the repo and only the operator one looked to have this log config ordering issue

signal.title: standalone-dns-proxy: return an error when no endpoint is found
signal.text: `LookupRegisteredEndpoint` reported a lookup miss as (nil, false, nil). The shared `ServeDNS` caller only inspects the returned error before using the endpoint, so it dereferenced the nil endpoint and panicked the whole proxy: ``` panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference github.com/cilium/cilium/pkg/endpoint.(*Endpoint).StringID(...) pkg/endpoint/endpoint.go:848 github.com/cilium/cilium/pkg/fqdn/dnsproxy.(*DNSProxy).ServeDNS(...) pkg/fqdn/dnsproxy/proxy.go:983 ``` The IP to endpoint table is a snapshot replicated from the agent, so an endpoint can in principle send a DNS request before its IP has been received. This has not been observed in steady state, but it becomes likely during a burst of endpoint creation: starting a batch of pods selected by a `toFQDNs` policy on a single node reproduced it consistently, with the new pods' source IPs still absent from the table while they were already resolving. Because the panic takes down the proxy process, a single such request breaks DNS for every endpoint on the node. The agent's own implementation of this interface always returns a non-nil error when it cannot resolve an endpoint, which is why only the standalone DNS proxy was affected. Match that contract so a miss is reported as an error, and the request is answered with SERVFAIL instead of crashing. AIL: 2 ```release-note standalone-dns-proxy: return an error when no endpoint is found ```
signal.author: vipul-21

signal.title: fix(gateway): fail closed on invalid ExternalAuth
signal.text: ## Description of change Make HTTPRoute ExternalAuth fail closed when the backend reference is invalid or cannot be resolved. Previously, an invalid ExternalAuth backend reference could cause the filter to be omitted while the route remained active, effectively allowing requests to bypass external authentication. This change: - Fails closed with HTTP 500 when the ExternalAuth backend reference is not permitted by a ReferenceGrant. - Fails closed when the ExternalAuth backend cannot be resolved. - Adds unit tests covering invalid cross-namespace references, missing backends, and valid ReferenceGrant configuration. Fixes: #47877 ```release-note Fix HTTPRoute ExternalAuth to fail closed when its backend reference is invalid or cannot be resolved. ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:3. signal.text: `setStaticAddressStatus` compared addresses from `Gateway.spec.addresses` with the generated Service status as strings. Parse both sides with `netip.ParseAddr` and compare the resulting addresses. Hostname-only Service ingress entries are ignored. signal.title: Cilium Gateway with Envoy rejects IPv6 PROXY headers from LB while IPv4 works
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.18.4 and lower than v1.19.0 ### What happened? I am using Cilium Gateway API with Envoy for HTTP(S) traffic. The Load Balancer is a Hetzner Cloud LB (TCP mode) with Proxy Protocol enabled. The flow that breaks is as follows: ``` [IPv6 client] -> [Hetzner LoadBalancer] -> (proxy protocol) [IPv4 endpoint on the Kubernetes nodes] ``` With this setup: * IPv4 clients work correctly when Proxy Protocol is enabled. * IPv6 clients fail to connect (connection stalls/handshake never completes). The connection does reach Envoy, as it emits a warning for each IPv6-iniated request: `[21][warning][filter] [cilium/l7policy.cc:100] cilium.l7policy: Cilium policy filter state not found`. When we disable Proxy Protocol on the LB, then both IPv4 and IPv6 work normally. The same Hetzner LB + Proxy Protocol configuration previously worked fine with NGINX Ingress. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Create a Cilium cluster with: ```yaml gatewayAPI: enabled: true enableProxyProtocol: true enableAlpn: true enableAppProtocol: true externalTrafficPolicy: Local ``` 2. Deploy a Gateway + HTTPRoute to an existing service. 3. Attach a Hetzner LB in TCP mode, with PROXY protocol enabled. 4. Send traffic over IPv4 > works. 5. Send traffic over IPv6 > fails (no handshake). 6. Disable Proxy Protocol on the LB → IPv6 works immediately. 7. Re-enable Proxy Protocol > IPv6 fails again. ### Cilium Version v1.18.4 ### Kernel Version 6.12.57-talos ### Kubernetes Version Server Version: v1.34.0 ### Regression Unknown. Just starting to use Gateway API. ### Sysdump It fails to upload. Helm values: ```yaml ipam: mode: kubernetes hubble: relay: enabled: true ui: enabled: true hostFirewall: enabled: false kubeProxyReplacement: true k8s: requireIPv4PodCIDR: true securityContext: capabilities: ciliumAgent: - CHOWN - KILL - NET_ADMIN - NET_RAW - IPC_LOCK - SYS_ADMIN - SYS_RESOURCE - DAC_OVERRIDE - FOWNER - SETGID - SETUID cleanCiliumState: - NET_ADMIN - SYS_ADMIN - SYS_RESOURCE operator: replicas: 2 cgroup: autoMount: enabled: true hostRoot: /sys/fs/cgroup k8sServiceHost: localhost k8sServicePort: "7445" policyAuditMode: false ipv4: enabled: true mtu: 1350 gatewayAPI: enabled: true enableProxyProtocol: true enableAlpn: true enableAppProtocol: true externalTrafficPolicy: Local ``` ### Relevant log output ```shell ❯ openssl s_client -connect "[2a01:4f8:c01e:734::1]:443" -servername microblog.network Connecting to 2a01:4f8:c01e:734::1 CONNECTED(00000003) depth=2 C=US, O=Internet Security Research Group, CN=ISRG Root X1 verify return:1 depth=1 C=US, O=Let's Encrypt, CN=R12 verify return:1 depth=0 CN=microblog.network verify return:1 --- Certificate chain 0 s:CN=microblog.network i:C=US, O=Let's Encrypt, CN=R12 a:PKEY: RSA, 2048 (bit); sigalg: sha256WithRSAEncryption v:NotBefore: Nov 23 06:21:35 2025 GMT; NotAfter: Feb 21 06:21:34 2026 GMT 1 s:C=US, O=Let's Encrypt, CN=R12 i:C=US, O=Internet Security Research Group, CN=ISRG Root X1 a:PKEY: RSA, 2048 (bit); sigalg: sha256WithRSAEncryption v:NotBefore: Mar 13 00:00:00 2024 GMT; NotAfter: Mar 12 23:59:59 2027 GMT --- Server certificate [snip] subject=CN=microblog.network issuer=C=US, O=Let's Encrypt, CN=R12 --- No client certificate CA names sent Peer signing digest: SHA256 Peer signature type: rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 Peer Temp Key: X25519, 253 bits --- SSL handshake has read 3088 bytes and written 1628 bytes Verification: OK --- New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 Protocol: TLSv1.3 Server public key is 2048 bit This TLS version forbids renegotiation. Compression: NONE Expansion: NONE No ALPN negotiated Early data was not sent Verify return code: 0 (ok) # at this point I send the HTTP request: GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: microblog.network Connection: close # it closed the connection: RECONNECTING --- ``` ### Anything else? ^ Relevant log output shows an `openssl` command. Interesting thing here is that its able to reach the cluster, exchanges TLS, verifies the certificate but closes the connection when trying to complete the HTTP request. ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? signal.title: NetworkPolicy silently not enforced for pods carrying a label with key `host` (v1.20.0)
signal.text: ## Summary A Kubernetes pod carrying a label whose **key** is `host` has **all NetworkPolicy enforcement silently disabled**. The pod is not isolated and nothing anywhere reports a problem. The label's *value* is irrelevant. This is security-relevant: a workload that happens to use a `host` label (e.g. `host: <nodename>`, a common convention for pinning/labelling probes) silently loses its network isolation while passing every health check. ## Steps to reproduce Two pods that are identical except that one carries an extra `host` label, and two identical NetworkPolicies, each selecting its own pod by its `app` label: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: {name: lblbug} --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: {name: p-a, namespace: lblbug, labels: {app: p-a}} spec: containers: - {name: c, image: "registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.47", args: ["netexec","--http-port=8080"]} --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: {name: p-b, namespace: lblbug, labels: {app: p-b, host: anything}} spec: containers: - {name: c, image: "registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.47", args: ["netexec","--http-port=8080"]} --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: {name: cli, namespace: lblbug, labels: {app: cli}} spec: containers: - {name: c, image: "registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.47", command: ["sleep","infinity"]} --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: {name: iso-a, namespace: lblbug} spec: podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: p-a}} policyTypes: [Ingress] ingress: [{from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: nope}}}]}] --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: {name: iso-b, namespace: lblbug} spec: podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: p-b}} policyTypes: [Ingress] ingress: [{from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: nope}}}]}] ``` Then, from `cli`, reach each target on port 8080. **Expected:** both `p-a` and `p-b` are blocked — each is selected by a policy whose only ingress rule matches a label that exists on nothing. **Actual:** ``` p-a {app: p-a} -> BLOCKED (correct) p-b {app: p-b, host: anything} -> REACHABLE (policy not enforced) ``` ## Evidence `cilium-dbg endpoint list` on the node hosting both pods: ``` ENDPOINT POLICY (ingress) POLICY (egress) IDENTITY LABELS 1867 Enabled Disabled 12065 k8s:app=p-a 977 Disabled Disabled 7085 k8s:app=p-b ``` Everything upstream of enforcement looks correct for `p-b`: * the NetworkPolicy object is accepted; the agent logs `NetworkPolicy successfully added` * `cilium-dbg policy get` renders the rule correctly (`Tier: 200`, `"DefaultDeny": true`, `"Ingress": true`) * `cilium-dbg policy subject-selectors` resolves the rule's subject to **exactly that pod's identity**, `USERS=1` * the endpoint reaches the agent's current policy revision, state `ready`, no failing controllers Only `cilium-dbg statedb` (table `policy-computations`) dissents — and it reports **no error**: ``` Identity=12065 (p-a) IngressPolicyEnabled=true rev=2 ingressPortRules=256 Identity= 7085 (p-b) IngressPolicyEnabled=false rev=2 ingressPortRules=1 Err=null ``` The endpoint's BPF policy map for `p-b` holds a catch-all `Allow Ingress ANY`. ## Scope — only `host` One pod per candidate key, each with its own identical policy, all on the same node and namespace: ``` (no extra label) -> BLOCKED (enforced) host -> REACHABLE ** only failure ** world -> BLOCKED (enforced) health -> BLOCKED (enforced) init -> BLOCKED (enforced) remote-node -> BLOCKED (enforced) kube-apiserver -> BLOCKED (enforced) ``` So it is not reserved words generally — it is `host` specifically. ## Why this is easy to misdiagnose `PolicyEnforcement=always` is **also inert** on such a pod. Since `always` is defined to enforce default-deny on every endpoint irrespective of any rule, its failure reads as a broken cluster rather than a bad label — which is how we originally diagnosed it. It is consistent with the endpoint being treated as host-ish somewhere, given the host endpoint is exempt from policy unless the host firewall is enabled (`Host firewall: Disabled` here). This also means the usual checks all pass: the object exists, the agent logged success, translation is right, and the selector resolves to the right identity. Nothing surfaces the problem except the `policy-computations` table. ## Environment * Cilium **v1.20.0** (`v1.20.0-450c5314`), agent image digest `sha256:383968cd5e8873f7976fa76aa6196045643558f4cc9518a207b9335cb24a0e93` * Kubernetes 1.35.5 and 1.35.7 * Talos Linux v1.13.8, kernel `6.18.42-talos` * `kubeProxyReplacement=false` (kube-proxy retained), `ipam.mode=kubernetes`, routing mode tunnel/VXLAN, host firewall disabled, Hubble on a local socket * Reproduced on two independent clusters: a 10-node cluster (5 control planes) and a separate 5-node cluster (3 control planes) built from scratch ## What I have not tested All observations are on Talos Linux. I have **not** yet tried this on kind/minikube or another distro, so I cannot say whether it is substrate-independent — though nothing about the mechanism looks Talos-specific. Happy to add that if useful. ## Note The [Terminology docs](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/gettingstarted/terminology/) state that label keys are prefixed with their source (`k8s:role=frontend` vs `reserved:host`) specifically to disambiguate user labels from reserved ones, which suggests a pod's `k8s:host=x` should never be conflated with the `reserved:host` identity. I could not find an existing issue or any documented restriction on using `host` as a pod label key.

signal.title: renovate: Fix primary GID of the ubuntu user and restore builder.sh root check
signal.text: ## Summary The `ubuntu` user in `ghcr.io/renovatebot/renovate` is defined with primary GID 0: ```console $ docker run --rm ghcr.io/renovatebot/renovate:43.176.5 grep ubuntu /etc/passwd ubuntu:x:12021:0::/home/ubuntu:/bin/bash ``` so Renovate and everything it spawns run as `12021:0`, and `builder.sh` takes the temporary root path added in #45663 instead of its normal UID/GID remapping. ## Changes **1. Swap the ubuntu user's primary group before dropping privileges** (`.github/actions/renovate/entrypoint.sh`) ```sh if [ "$(id -gn ubuntu)" = "root" ]; then usermod -aG root ubuntu usermod -g ubuntu ubuntu fi ``` Renovate then runs as `12021:12021`, with root kept as a supplementary group. **2. Create `/home/ubuntu/.cache` in the builder container before chowning it** (`contrib/scripts/builder.sh`) When no cache directory gets mounted (e.g. Go is not installed on the host, as in the Renovate image), `/home/ubuntu/.cache` doesn't exist and the unconditional `chown` fails under `set -eu`. A `mkdir -p` before the `chown` fixes this for every caller. **3. Remove the temporary root workaround and block root explicitly** (`contrib/scripts/builder.sh`) With the GID fixed, the workaround from #45663 is no longer needed. Running with UID or GID 0 now fails early, so an accidental root run can't reassign GID 0 files inside the container. ## Testing Verified end to end with a live Renovate run on a fork, using this branch's entrypoint and `builder.sh`, without `BUILDER_GOCACHE_DIR`. The genuine `postUpgradeTask` on the `renovate/all-go-deps-main` branch ran `contrib/scripts/builder.sh true` to completion: - `runuser -u ubuntu -- id` → `uid=12021(ubuntu) gid=12021(ubuntu) groups=12021(ubuntu),0(root),118(docker_group)` - `builder.sh` took the normal UID/GID remapping path (the new root check never fired), `mkdir -p /home/ubuntu/.cache` ran, and the `chown` that used to fail succeeded; rc=0. This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally verified the container group membership behavior and the end-to-end Renovate runs described above. Fixes: #45663 ```release-note Fix the Renovate entrypoint to run with the ubuntu group instead of GID 0, and restore builder.sh's rejection of root. ```

signal.title: node/manager: Populate node table from manager
signal.text: We're on regular basis now encountering the situation where we would like to be able to fetch and watch information about individual Cilium nodes in the agent. Currently this requires implementing a `node.Handler` and subscribing with the `NodeManager` which is fair bit of boilerplate and annoying to test. It's even worse if all the rest of the code is interacting with StateDB tables. As a first small step towards https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/41744 and to allow new code to easily watch and look up nodes, change the `Table[*LocalNode]` into `Table[*Node]` and populate the remote nodes into this table from `NodeManager`. This PR tries to keep the changes to a minimum and local to `pkg/node` and hence uses adds a `type LocalNode = Node` alias and doesn't change the `LocalNodeStoreCell` structure. The runtime impact of this change without further cleanup is that we now temporarily have an additional index for remote Cilium nodes and we store`types.Node` twice (shallow clone, 296 bytes). The next step would be to refactor `NodeManager` to use `Table[*Node]` internally to avoid the duplicate indexing.

signal.title: docs: document Envoy listener redirect and wildcard port in L4 policy
signal.text: Add a section to the Layer 4 policy docs covering the toPorts listener field, which redirects matching egress traffic to a named Envoy listener defined in a CiliumEnvoyConfig or CiliumClusterwideEnvoyConfig. Includes three examples: a header-injection redirect, an external forward proxy with Proxy-Authorization, and a wildcard-port (port 0) variant that redirects all internet-bound egress. Documents the egress-only and no-L7-rules constraints, the use-original-source-address annotation, built-in egress-cluster routing, credential handling limits, and recommends Gateway API/GAMMA for cases they cover. Cross-links the L7 traffic management page. ```release-note docs: document Envoy listener redirect and wildcard port in L4 policy ``` cc @jrajahalme
signal.author: PhilipSchmid

signal.title: bpf: don't reclassify an already reverse-NATed service reply
signal.text: - [X] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [X] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [X] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [X] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [X] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [X] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [X] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. - [X] Thanks for contributing! <!-- Description of change --> On netkit + endpointRoutes + per-packet LB, a service reply is evaluated twice on the client's ingress path. The first pass matches conntrack and reverse-NATs the source to the service address; the packet is then re-delivered and evaluated again, now carrying an address that doesn't match the backend-keyed CT entry, and gets classified CT_NEW. This produces a spurious CT entry, a false Hubble flow showing the client as its own destination on an ephemeral port, and, with an ingress policy on the client, Policy denied drops of established connections' replies. Set a flag on ctx->tc_index after lb{4,6}_rev_nat() reverse-NATs a CT_REPLY packet; cil_to_container() reads and clears it on re-entry and delivers directly instead of re-running ingress. tc_index is used because it's the only per-packet state that survives the re-entry: CB_DELIVERY_FLAGS is cleared by bpf_clear_meta() and skb->mark is consumed by inherit_identity_from_host(), both confirmed via cilium-dbg monitor -v with Debug/DebugLB enabled. Fixes: #47913 ```release-note bpf: fix spurious CT_NEW reclassification of service replies on netkit with endpoint routes and per-packet load balancing, which caused incorrect Hubble flows and could drop replies to established connections under an ingress CiliumNetworkPolicy. ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:4. I personally validated the resulting network flows with and without policies, both visually via Hubble and by testing the affected applications. I could not find an existing test in the suite combining netkit + endpointRoutes + per-packet LB. Every netkit test that I found has per_packet_lb=0. Three tests enable per-packet LB and exercise bpf_lxc (skip_lb_xlate_lrp_per_packet_lb.c, tc_nodeport_lb_fragments.h, tc_lb_external_ips.h), but all three are netkit=0, endpoint_routes=0. The problem is easily reproducible (see #47913) and the fix is only a few simple lines, so building out a full test harness for netkit=1, endpoint_routes=1 seems disproportionate in this case, and I don't have the background in the code to know that the test case would be right. It was very obvious that the fix addressed the problem without obviously creating new problems (via Hubble UI, policies and applications working again).

signal.title: cilium-cli: respect --ip-families in validateDeployment
signal.text: NodePort readiness checks and secondary network IP collection were gated only on cluster-enabled IP families, ignoring --ip-families. signal.title: ci: resolve renovate PR metadata in base image workflows
signal.text: The base image push step relied on github.event.pull_request metadata to detect Renovate-authored PRs and temporarily re-draft them before pushing follow-up image updates. The reason behind this is to prevent unnecessary notifications / reviews from users. These reviews should already be handled by `ciliumbot`. That works for pull_request_target runs, but not for the workflow_call path used by the Renovate branch workflows, where github.event.pull_request is unset. In that case pr_number and pr_author were empty, so the workflow skipped the re-draft logic. Since this usecase is the relevant one, this commit fixes this by falling back to resolving the PR from the branch name with `gh pr list --head` when PR metadata is missing. Use the short ref name for the non-PR path so the branch lookup matches correctly. Note: we need to accept both Renovate author formats: - `cilium-renovate[bot]` from PR webhook payloads - `app/cilium-renovate` from `gh pr list` GraphQL output See PR: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/47950 and related [workflow run](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/actions/runs/31743959287/job/94593874945) that didn't draft the PR as intended. Fixes: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/47364

Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! <!-- Description of change --> `peerConfig` in the WireGuard agent was keeping each allowed IP in two places at once: ```go allowedIPs map[netip.Prefix]net.IPNet needsInsert map[netip.Prefix]net.IPNet needsRemove map[netip.Prefix]net.IPNet ``` The key and the value are the same prefix, just encoded differently. The `net.IPNet` half is there because `wgtypes.PeerConfig.AllowedIPs` is a `[]net.IPNet`, so the package was carrying the wgctrl representation through its own state rather than converting at the edge. This turns the three maps into sets keyed by `netip.Prefix` and moves the `net.IPNet` conversion out to the two spots that talk to wgctrl. A few other things follow from that: - `ipnetToPrefix()` called `netipx.MustFromStdIP()`, which panics if the IP is not 4 or 16 bytes. The replacement uses `netipx.FromStdIP()` and callers skip the prefix if the conversion fails. - Four blocks were building a `/32` or `/128` by hand with `net.CIDRMask()` plus an IPv4/IPv6 branch. `netip.Addr.BitLen()` already gives the right width, so those become one helper call each. Left alone on purpose: `peerConfig.nodeIPv4`/`nodeIPv6` are still `net.IP`. Converting them touches ~100 more sites in the tests and would bury this change. The `fakeWgClient` helpers and the `wgtypes.PeerConfig` literals in `cell_test.go` also stay on `net.IPNet`, since that is the API they are standing in for. Related: #24246 ## Testing `pkg/wireguard/agent` has no privileged tests, so the existing suite covers this locally end to end: ``` $ go build ./... $ go vet ./pkg/wireguard/... $ go test ./pkg/wireguard/... ok github.com/cilium/cilium/pkg/wireguard/agent 0.025s $ golangci-lint run pkg/wireguard/... 0 issues. $ gofmt -s -l pkg/wireguard/agent/ ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:1. signal.title: node-init startup script fails on GKE >= 1.36.2-gke.2064000: GKE-containerd probe no longer matches node image
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.0 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? After GKE auto-upgraded cluster nodes from `1.36.2-gke.1498000` to `1.36.2-gke.2064000` (Rapid channel, 2026-R32 rollout), every `cilium-node-init` pod crash-looped and no cilium agent ever started, causing a cluster-wide outage. Node-init logs: ``` [pod/cilium-node-init-mpzc5/node-init] Device "cbr0" does not exist. [pod/cilium-node-init-mpzc5/node-init] bash: line 121: kubelet: command not found [pod/cilium-node-init-mpzc5/node-init] !!! startup-script failed! exit code '127' ``` ### Root cause The startup script's GKE-containerd probe ```bash if [[ -f "${GKE_KUBERNETES_BIN_DIR}/gke" ]] && [[ $(grep -cF -- '--container-runtime-endpoint' "${KUBELET_DEFAULTS_FILE}") == "1" ]]; then ``` no longer matches on the `gke.2064000` node image. Kubelet still *runs with* the `--container-runtime-endpoint="unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock"` flag (visible in the node journal), so GKE apparently assembles kubelet flags elsewhere now and `/etc/default/kubelet` no longer contains it (or the `gke` marker file is gone — node shell access is restricted on GKE, so I could not determine which of the two conditions fails). The script then falls into the generic branch, which runs: ```bash K8S_VERSION=$(kubelet --version) ``` `kubelet` is not in the PATH of the startup-script container (it lives at `/home/kubernetes/bin/kubelet` on the host), so this exits 127. With `set -o errexit` the script dies before writing `/tmp/cilium-bootstrap.d/cilium-bootstrap-time`, so the agent's `wait-for-node-init` init container blocks forever. Result: no CNI, `cilium-agent-not-ready` taint never cleared, nothing schedules — a full cluster deadlock that also takes down konnectivity (no kubectl logs/exec) and any admission webhook with `failurePolicy: Fail`. Note the fallback branch is unreachable by design: it invokes a bare `kubelet`, which the container never has in PATH, so *any* probe miss necessarily produces this outcome. The identical script is still on `main`: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/install/kubernetes/cilium/files/nodeinit/startup.bash ### Environment - cilium 1.19.6 via Helm chart, `nodeinit.enabled=true`, `reconfigureKubelet=true`, `removeCbrBridge=true` - GKE Rapid channel, regional cluster - Broken node image: `gke-1362-gke2064000-cos-129-19506-299-3-c-pre` (kernel 6.12.94, containerd 2.2.3) - Working node image: `gke-1362-gke1498000-cos-129-19506-224-80-c-pre` (kernel 6.12.90, containerd 2.2.3) - Downgrade to the working version is not possible — GKE removed it from valid versions ### Suggested fix - Make the probe robust, e.g. key on `/home/kubernetes/bin/kubelet` existing (GKE-specific path) instead of / in addition to the current markers; and/or - Use an absolute path (`/home/kubernetes/bin/kubelet --version`) or a PATH-safe guard in the fallback branch so a probe miss degrades gracefully instead of deadlocking the cluster. ### Workaround we are using Restore both markers before the probe via the chart's `nodeinit.startup.preScript` hook: ```bash touch /home/kubernetes/bin/gke if ! grep -qF -- '--container-runtime-endpoint' /etc/default/kubelet 2>/dev/null; then echo 'KUBELET_OPTS="${KUBELET_OPTS:-} --container-runtime-endpoint=unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock"' >> /etc/default/kubelet fi ``` This makes the probe pass on both the old and the new node image and preserves the kubelet wrapper. Disabling `reconfigureKubelet` also avoids the crash but loses the wrapper (reboot persistence for the containerd `conf_template` workaround), so we avoided that. ### How can we reproduce the issue (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. GKE Rapid cluster on `1.36.2-gke.2064000` (or let nodes auto-upgrade to it) 2. Install cilium Helm chart with `nodeinit.enabled=true`, `nodeinit.reconfigureKubelet=true` 3. Watch `cilium-node-init` pods crash-loop with exit 127; `cilium` agent pods stuck at `Init:4/7` (`wait-for-node-init`)

signal.title: install: detect GKE from kubelet path
signal.text: GKE `1.36.2-gke.2064000` no longer exposes the container runtime endpoint through the `--container-runtime-endpoint` flag in `/etc/default/kubelet`. This causes the existing node-init GKE detection to miss the GKE-specific path and fall through to generic kubelet handling. Instead of detecting individual GKE node layouts through container runtime configuration, this change uses the presence of `/home/kubernetes/bin/kubelet`, which is shared by both the legacy and current GKE layouts. The same detection is used by startup and prestop, so the kubelet wrapper installed during startup can also be detected and reverted correctly. Testing performed: * `helm lint` * Helm template rendering with GKE/node-init values * `bash -n` on rendered startup and prestop scripts * sandboxed scenarios covering legacy GKE, the GKE 1.36.2 layout, generic non-GKE nodes, and an already-installed kubelet wrapper * live GKE `1.36.2-gke.2064000` COS/containerd node verification: * `/home/kubernetes/bin/kubelet` exists as a regular executable file * `/home/kubernetes/kubelet-config.yaml` contains `containerRuntimeEndpoint: unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock` * `/etc/default/kubelet` does not contain `--container-runtime-endpoint` * `git diff --check` Claude was used to suggest the implementation. I manually reviewed the changes and validated the resulting behavior with the tests above. AIL:4 Fixes: #47884 ```release-note Fix node-init startup on GKE 1.36.2-gke.2064000 nodes by detecting GKE from the kubelet path instead of container runtime configuration. ```

signal.title: pkg/mtu: Add fallback to MTU of 1500 and identify the primary ENI by device index
signal.text: In ENI IPAM mode the MTU auto detection excludes the secondary ENIs, which are managed by Cilium, and derives the base MTU from the primary ENI only. The primary ENI was told apart from the secondary ones by comparing ENI.IP with the first NodeInternalIP of the CiliumNode. ENI.IP is the primary private IPv4 address of the ENI, as reported by the EC2 API, so on a node whose first NodeInternalIP is an IPv6 address no ENI ever matched and every device was excluded, including the primary one. With no device left, the base MTU stayed at its MaxMTU initializer and Cilium tried to configure an MTU of 65520, which the ENA driver rejects. Use the ENI device index instead, as the AWS IPAM code already does. It is address family agnostic and does not depend on the ordering of the node addresses. This also adds a fallback to the default Ethernet MTU (1500 bytes) when no device is left to detect the MTU from, so that a filtering mistake cannot result in an unusable MTU again. **This part impacts all IPAM modes not just ENI IPAM.** This PR was prepared with AIL:3. ```release-note pkg/mtu: Added a fallback to an MTU of 1500 bytes if no network devices are selected for MTU detection. Fixed a bug where Cilium would fail to find the appropriate MTU to use when in IPAM ENI mode with IPv6 enabled. ```
signal.author: 41ks

signal.title: ciliumidentity: include named-port labels in operator-managed identities
signal.text: Fixes: #47214 Pods with named container ports get stuck in ContainerCreating when identityManagementMode=operator. The root cause is a mismatch between how the agent and the operator build the CiliumIdentity key for such pods. The agent includes a gen:io.cilium.k8s.named-ports label in the key, derived from the pod's named container ports. The operator did not, because it called GetCIDKeyFromLabels on the raw k8s label map without ever calling GetPodMetadata, so the named ports were never seen. With different keys, the operator allocates an identity the agent never looks up, and the agent waits for an identity the operator never creates. CNI endpoint creation times out and the pod stays stuck. AIL: 0

signal.title: cli: ignore ENI IPv6 beta warning and detect IPv6 EKS server URL
signal.text: # Ignoring the beta warning The ENI IPv6 implementation is in beta for the v1.20 release of Cilium. This adds the beta warning log to the list of expected warnings in the CLI. Otherwise, the error check test fails when running connectivity tests with ENI+IPv6 enabled. Example test error: ``` . ❌ Found 1 logs in [...]/my-ipv6-cluster/kube-system/cilium-operator-b8c85f56b-txldk (cilium-operator) matching list of errors that must be investigated: time=2026-07-27T15:48:15.96359495Z level=warn msg="IPv6 support in the ENI IPAM mode (ipam.mode=eni, ipv6.enabled=true) is a beta feature. Please use it with caution and report any issues you encounter: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/new?template=bug_report.yaml" subsys=cilium-operator-aws (1 occurrences) ``` The error no longer appears after this change. # Detecting EKS IPv6 server URL For IPv6 EKS clusters, the format of the server URL is different than that of IPv4 clusters. For IPv6, the URL is suffixed with eks-cluster.\<region\>.api.aws (See https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/cluster-endpoint.html#cluster-endpoint-ipv6). This change relaxes detection of EKS flavor by server endpoint URL. The new condition should match all types of EKS clusters (Commercial, GovCloud, China) (IPv4, IPv6). However, I did note some inconsistencies in the AWS docs as in IPv4 I get this pattern `https://ABCDEF1234567890.gr7.us-west-2.eks.amazonaws.com` while on IPv6 I get the `eks-cluster` substring `https://ABCDEF1234567890.gr7.eks-cluster.us-west-2.api.aws`. signal.title: bpf: stop dropping MLD and router solicitation sent from pods
signal.text: Pods keep showing up in Hubble as dropping their own ICMPv6 traffic with "Invalid source ip". The source is always the link local address that the kernel gives the pod interface, and the messages are the MLD reports and router solicitations that the kernel sends on its own. The from container path lets neighbour solicitation and neighbour advertisement past the source IP check and nothing else, so all of this gets treated as spoofed. The packets are link scoped and cannot reach anything anyway, so nothing is actually broken, but the drop counters and flow logs make it look like the pod is misbehaving. This change lets MLD and router solicitation through when the source is a link local or unspecified address and the destination is a link local scope multicast group. Those packets go to the stack instead of being routed anywhere. Router advertisement and redirect are deliberately left out, since a pod has no reason to send either one and both are useful to an attacker. There is a new BPF unit test with six cases, three that should now pass and three that must stay dropped. I checked it works both ways by reverting each half of the change and watching only the matching tests fail. Fixes: #47645 ```release-note Stop dropping MLD and router solicitation messages that pods send from their kernel assigned link local address when source IP verification is enabled ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:4. I reviewed the datapath change, and ran the BPF unit tests and checkpatch locally.
